title: Plotinus in modern English
author: Plotinus
label: The Workshop's modern English, machine-assisted: drafted with an AI model (Claude) from the Greek and not yet checked by a scholar. Taylor's English of each chapter is one tap away.
about: A modern English version of Plotinus, written for the Workshop. It is translated from the Greek of Volkmann's edition (Leipzig, 1883-1884), as First1KGreek gives it, chapter by chapter, and checked against Thomas Taylor's translation of 1817. Where the Greek says something Taylor's English does not, the modern version follows the Greek, and a flag shows Taylor's words and the difference. Plato's words that Plotinus quotes are noted with their place. The chapters are Volkmann's (Ficino's); the short titles and summaries are the Workshop's. It covers all fifteen treatises that Taylor translated, in Porphyry's order, from I.2, On the Virtues, to VI.9, On the Good, or the One.

treatises.title: On the virtues
treatises.summary: Plato says we should escape from this world by becoming like God, through virtue. But God has no need of virtues. Plotinus answers that we can become like something that does not itself have what makes us like it, as a house is like the plan of it. He then sets the virtues in two ranks: the civic virtues, which put measure into our desires and feelings, and the greater virtues, which purify the soul and turn it to intellect. The good person lives by the greater, and his aim is to live the life of the gods, not just the life of a good human being.

treatises.title: On dialectic
treatises.summary: What leads us up to the Good? Plato names three kinds of people who can be led up: the musician, the lover and the philosopher. Each starts from a different place, and Plotinus says how each is to be led. All of them must come at last to dialectic, which is not a tool for arguing but the highest part of philosophy: knowledge of what each thing is, which rests in the intelligible world and hands logic over to others. The lower virtues and wisdom grow together and complete each other.

treatises.title: On matter
treatises.summary: Everyone who has thought about matter agrees that it is a substrate, a receiver of forms; they differ about what it is. Plotinus first argues that there is a matter in the intelligible world too: the depth beneath the forms there, unbounded until it turns to the One. He then turns to the matter of bodies. It is needed because the elements change into one another; it has no quality and no size, and is known only by a "bastard reasoning". It is not a quality, nor a privation added to something else: it is the unlimited itself, poverty itself, and so evil.

treatises.title: Against the Gnostics
treatises.summary: Against those who say the maker of the world is evil and the world bad: the Gnostics among Plotinus' own hearers. There are three principles and no more: the Good, intellect and soul. The world was made not by a fallen soul, nor by reasoning, but by soul's contemplation of what is above it; it is the best possible image of the intelligible, and the stars have souls better than ours. The Gnostics borrow from Plato and spoil it, despise the gods, call themselves God's only sons, and teach no virtue. The good person lives here calmly, as in a fine house another built.

treatises.title: On the impassibility of things without body
treatises.summary: How can the soul, which has no body, be free from affection, when it seems to feel pleasure and pain, fear and desire, and to change with virtue and vice? Plotinus answers that perception, memory and virtue are activities, not imprints; the feelings belong to the body or to the living compound, with soul as their cause; and purification is the soul's waking from images. Then matter: it too is untouched. It is not being but a phantom, a mirror in which images come and go and leave no trace, "the receptacle and nurse" of becoming, which takes on nothing and keeps nothing.

treatises.title: On eternity and time
treatises.summary: We seem to know what eternity and time are until we try to say. Eternity is not intelligible being, nor rest, but the life of being all at once, whole, with no past or future. Time is not motion, nor what is moved, nor an interval or measure of motion, as the earlier schools said. It began when soul, restless to put what it saw into another, stepped out of eternity: time is the life of soul moving from one way of life to another, the image of eternity, and the world is in it.

treatises.title: On the essence of the soul
treatises.summary: A short treatise on the soul's essence. Having shown elsewhere that the soul is not a body, Plotinus places it among the intelligibles and goes further. Bodies are wholly divided, intellect wholly undivided; between them are forms and qualities divided in bodies, and soul, divided about bodies because present in every part, yet undivided because whole in each. This is Plato's third kind of being, mixed from the undivided and the divided. Sensation proves it: if soul were divided like a body, one part would not feel what another suffers; if simply one, it would give life to no body.

treatises.title: On difficulties about the soul (I)
treatises.summary: The first of three books of problems about the soul, and the longest treatise Taylor translated. Are our souls parts of the world's soul? No: all souls are one and many as the theorems of one science, sisters from one soul. Soul is not in body as in a place or vessel, nor as form in matter, but body is in soul, like air in light. Souls come down, each at its time, by a natural law, to the body made ready for them. Last, memory belongs to soul, not body, and to both imagining powers; going up, the soul forgets more and more.

treatises.title: On the immortality of the soul
treatises.summary: Is each of us immortal? A man is soul and body; the body, being composite, perishes, and the man himself is the soul. Against the Stoics and atomists, Plotinus argues that soul is not a body: no body lives of itself; perceiving needs one undivided thing that takes in the whole; thinking grasps what has no size; virtue and justice are not bodies. Nor is soul a harmony, as the Pythagoreans said, nor an entelechy, as Aristotle said: it is a being that lives of itself. Being of the divine, everlasting kind, as its love of wisdom shows, it is immortal.

treatises.title: On the three principal hypostases
treatises.summary: Why have souls forgotten their father, God? Daring, birth and the wish to be their own carried them away, and admiring what is here they despised themselves. The cure is to remind the soul of its worth. Plotinus leads it up: the soul that makes and moves the whole heaven, like ours; above it intellect, the true world, eternal, which is being; above that the One, which produces intellect without moving, as the sun gives light. These three were already in Plato and Parmenides, and they are in us too. To see the One we must turn inward and wait, as for the sunrise.

treatises.title: On the generation and order of things after the first
treatises.summary: A short treatise on the going out of all things from the One. The One is all things and none of them: because nothing is in it, all comes from it. Perfect, it overflowed, and what came from it turned back and looked to it, and so became being and intellect. Intellect in turn poured out power, and soul came to be; soul, moving, produced its image, perception and the nature in plants. Each stays in its own seat while what it produces takes a lower rank, so that all is like one long life stretched out, each part different, nothing cut off.

treatises.title: On the knowing hypostases, and what is beyond
treatises.summary: Can the simple think itself, or must what thinks itself be complex? Plotinus begins with the soul: perception looks outward, the reasoning part judges by rules from intellect, and we are this reasoning part, with perception our messenger and intellect our king. True self-knowledge belongs to intellect, where seeing and seen are one; we know it by becoming it. But intellect, two in one, cannot be first: before it is the One, which does not think and is none of the things that are, known only by a touch beyond thought. The treatise ends with the cry: "Take away everything."

treatises.title: That what is beyond being does not think
treatises.summary: A short, tight argument. What thinks itself is both one and two: one, so that it has what it thinks as its own; two, so that it has something to think. Intellect is this. But what is first must be wholly one, needing nothing; thinking is a need and a movement towards the good, and it brings doubleness with it, a thinker and a thought, being and life and thinking together. So the first, the good, does not think, not even itself: it is beyond being and so beyond thinking, and gives other things something better than knowing them, the power to touch it.

treatises.title: On intellect, the forms, and being
treatises.summary: Most people live by perception and take pleasure for the good; some rise a little and fall back into practical virtue; a divine few see the light above and stay there as at home. The way up is the lover's and the philosopher's: from beautiful bodies to souls, from soul to the intellect that gives it wisdom. Intellect must exist before soul, always in act, and is itself the beings it thinks, the forms, all together yet distinct. There are forms of everything natural, of the arts that use reason, of man and of soul, but not of evil.

treatises.title: On the good, or the One
treatises.summary: Porphyry put this treatise last, the summit of the Enneads. Everything is by being one: an army, a house, a body, health, beauty, virtue. But the One is not soul, nor intellect, nor being, all of which are many; it is the formless source of all, known not by knowledge but by a presence better than knowledge. To approach it, let go of all shape, turn inward, become one, and wait. The soul's natural love is for the good; when it sees, seer and seen are no longer two: "the flight of the alone to the alone".

chapters.title: Becoming like God: does God have virtues?
chapters.summary: We escape evil by becoming like God. But which god, and does he have the virtues? The world-soul, who has nothing to fear and nothing to desire, cannot have courage or self-control. Then we are made like what does not have virtue: as the house we see is like the house in the mind, which has no need of order.

chapters.title: Two kinds of likeness; the civic virtues
chapters.summary: Likeness is of two kinds: between two copies of one original, and between a copy and its original. The civic virtues give measure to our desires and feelings, and so carry a trace of the measure above; the soul, nearer to the divine than the body, can seem a god itself.

chapters.title: The greater virtues are purifications
chapters.summary: Plato calls the virtues purifications, so there are two kinds. The soul is bad when it is mixed up with the body; it is good when it thinks on its own, does not share the body's feelings, does not fear to leave it, and lets reason lead. This is likeness to God. But God is not in a state of virtue: virtue belongs to the soul, not to intellect or what is beyond it.

chapters.title: Purification, turning, and the soul's own good
chapters.summary: Is virtue the purifying, or the having been purified? Purification only removes what is foreign; the soul's good is to be with what is akin to it, and it reaches it by turning. Its virtue is what comes from the turning: a seeing of the realities, whose imprints the soul held unlit and now lights up.

chapters.title: How far purification goes
chapters.summary: The purified soul draws itself together away from the body. It takes bodily pleasures only as cures, bears pain calmly, removes anger and fear as far as it can, and desires nothing base. It wants to make its lower part pure too, so that this part respects reason, as a man respects a wise neighbour.

chapters.title: To be a god, not only without fault
chapters.summary: The aim is not to be free from fault but to be a god. In the purified person wisdom is the seeing of what intellect holds. Each virtue is twofold: in intellect it is not virtue but the pattern; in the soul it is virtue. The greater justice, self-control and courage are the soul's activity towards intellect, its turning inward, and its freedom from passion.

chapters.title: The virtues follow one another; the life of the gods
chapters.summary: The virtues go together in the soul, as their patterns do in intellect. Whoever has the greater virtues has the lesser ones in potential. The good person will use the lesser when circumstances call for them, but will live by the higher measures, and choose not the life of a good human being but the life of the gods.

chapters.title: Who can be led up, and the musician
chapters.summary: The journey has two stages: up to the intelligible world, and then through it to its summit. Plato names three natures fit for the first: the musician, the lover and the philosopher. The musician, stirred by beautiful sounds, must be taught that what moved him was the harmony and beauty of the intelligible world.

chapters.title: The lover
chapters.summary: The lover remembers beauty but cannot grasp it apart from bodies. He must be led, as in Plato's Symposium, from one beautiful body to all of them, then to beautiful ways of life and laws, arts, sciences and virtues, and from the virtues up to intellect and being.

chapters.title: The philosopher
chapters.summary: The philosopher by nature is already winged and moving upward, and needs only to be shown the way: first mathematics, to train him in thinking of what has no body; then the completion of his virtues; then dialectic.

chapters.title: What dialectic is
chapters.summary: Dialectic is the power to say of each thing what it is, how it differs from others and what it shares with them, and to do this by knowledge, not opinion. It works in the intelligible world, dividing and combining the Forms until it reaches the first principle; then it rests, and leaves logic to another art.

chapters.title: Where dialectic gets its principles; dialectic and philosophy
chapters.summary: Intellect gives dialectic its principles. Dialectic is the most valuable part of philosophy, not a tool: it deals with real things, judges falsehood by the truth it holds, and leaves the fine points of propositions to another art.

chapters.title: The other parts of philosophy, and the natural virtues
chapters.summary: Philosophy also studies nature and conduct, with help from dialectic. Practical wisdom reasons about the virtues as a whole; dialectic and wisdom serve it from above. The lower virtues are incomplete without wisdom, and wisdom cannot come without them: the two grow together.

chapters.title: What the schools say matter is
chapters.summary: All agree that matter is a substrate and a receiver of forms, but not what it is. The Stoics, who hold that only bodies exist, make matter the one substance under the elements, a body without quality, and even make God matter in a certain state. Others call it incorporeal, and some posit a second matter in the intelligible world, under the forms there.

chapters.title: Objections to a matter in the intelligible world
chapters.summary: If matter is unbounded and formless, it cannot be among the best things there; simple things need no matter; only things that come to be need it. And where would it come from? If it was made, something made it; if it is eternal, there are many first principles; and form added to it would make a body there.

chapters.title: The unbounded is not always to be despised
chapters.summary: Not everything unbounded and shapeless is to be scorned, if it offers itself to what is better, as soul does to intellect. Composition there is not like that of bodies. The matter of things that come to be takes one form after another; the matter there has all forms at once, and so is never without form.

chapters.title: Why there must be matter there
chapters.summary: If there are many Forms, they have something in common and something of their own; what is their own is their shape, and what is shaped is matter. The world here imitates that world, and this one is made of matter, so that one has matter too. Take away from intellect its variety, shapes and thoughts, and what is left before them is shapeless and unbounded.

chapters.title: The depth of each thing; the matter there
chapters.summary: Intellect divides each thing till it reaches what is simple; the depth of each is matter, and so all matter is dark. The matter there has a defined and thinking life; the matter here becomes a defined but dead thing. The matter there comes from Otherness, the first motion, which is unbounded until it turns to the One and is lit by it.

chapters.title: Why bodies need a substrate
chapters.summary: The elements change into one another, so something must remain under the change: what perishes is never wholly destroyed, and nothing comes from what wholly is not. Perishing, induction and analysis all show that bodies are composite, of matter and form. The elements are not form alone, nor first matter, so they are made of both.

chapters.title: Against Empedocles, Anaxagoras, the infinite and atoms
chapters.summary: Empedocles' elements perish, so they are not matter. Anaxagoras' mixture, which has everything already, does away with the intellect he brings in. The infinite cannot be matter, whether as a thing by itself or as an attribute of a body. Atoms do not exist, since every body can be divided, and nothing continuous or living could be made of them.

chapters.title: Matter has no quality and no size
chapters.summary: Matter is not a body, since a body has quality. Being the matter of all sensible things, it has none of their properties: no colour, heat, weight or shape, and no size either. It must be simple. The forming principle brings size with it, as it brings quality; for each kind the form fixes its size.

chapters.title: Quantity is a form
chapters.summary: Not everything that exists has size: nothing incorporeal does, and matter is incorporeal. Quantity itself is not a quantity; what shares in it is. As what makes a thing white is not white, what makes a thing so big is not so big but the principle of size. It does not unroll matter into size; it gives it size it did not have.

chapters.title: How matter is thought: a bastard reasoning
chapters.summary: How can we think what has no size and no quality? By a kind of unboundedness in the soul, as darkness is the eye's matter. The account of it is bounded, but the soul's grasp of it is not; so its image is "bastard", as Plato says. The soul thinks it dimly, by not thinking, and quickly puts form on it again, afraid of being outside the things that are.

chapters.title: Matter is not bulk, but has a phantom of bulk
chapters.summary: Some say that if matter has no size it contributes nothing, and bodies need no matter. But a receiver need not have bulk: soul receives everything without it. Matter receives its forms in extension because it can receive extension. It has a phantom of bulk: great and small at once, running from one to the other, which is why some called it the void.

chapters.title: Matter is needed, and known by reasoning, not sense
chapters.summary: Forms of bodies are in sizes, but about something sized, other than size; otherwise there would be only rational principles in soul, and no bodies. Actions need no matter, but bodies are composite. So matter is not an empty name. It is grasped by no sense, but by an empty reasoning, a bastard one; and it has no bodiliness either.

chapters.title: Matter is not a quality, not even a privation
chapters.summary: If the substrate were a common quality, how could a quality be a substrate? Someone says matter is qualified by having no quality, as a blind man is qualified by blindness. But privation is not a quality; it is an absence, like silence. Matter's own character is just what it is: to be other than everything else, or rather "others".

chapters.title: Is matter privation?
chapters.summary: Is matter privation, or is privation in matter? Some say they are one in substrate, two in account. Then each account must be given. If they are separate, they are two; if like the snub nose, or fire and heat, they are still not one. If privation is a not-being, still there are two accounts. But if to be matter is to be unbounded and without quality, how are there two?

chapters.title: Matter is the unbounded itself
chapters.summary: The unbounded is not an attribute of matter: what orders is limit and principle, so what is ordered must be the unlimited, and an attribute must be a principle. So matter is the unlimited itself. In the intelligible world it is born of the One's infinite power; the matter here, an image fleeing from true being, is more truly unlimited.

chapters.title: Matter is poverty, and so evil
chapters.summary: Matter is not Otherness itself, but the part of Otherness opposed to the true beings, and so it is not-being and privation. Form coming to it does not destroy it, but brings it to what it is, as a seed sown or a female made pregnant. It is evil, not because it wants the good, but because it is poverty itself: of wisdom, virtue, beauty and form.

chapters.title: Three principles, and no more
chapters.summary: The Good is simple and first, the same as the One, with nothing above it. After it comes intellect, then soul: no fewer, since they differ, and no more. There is no intellect at rest beside one in motion, nor one that thinks beside one that thinks that it thinks, nor a rational principle between intellect and soul.

chapters.title: One intellect; and our soul in three parts
chapters.summary: There is one intellect, always the same, imitating its father as far as it can. Part of our soul is always with the things there, part with the things here, and part between; the lower part can drag down the middle, but not the whole. The soul of the universe never fell: it orders the world without effort, by looking at what is above it.

chapters.title: Everything gives of itself: the world has no beginning
chapters.summary: Lit always, soul always gives light to what follows, as a fire warms what is round it. Every principle must give of itself to another, or the Good would not be good, nor intellect intellect. So all things follow one another always: what is called "made" was always being made, and will not perish. Matter too is always lit.

chapters.title: The world-soul did not fall
chapters.summary: If they say the soul made the world when it lost its wings, the soul of the universe suffers no such thing. If it erred, when, and why then? It made the world not by sinking, but by not sinking; a forgetful soul could not make, and one that remembers would go back. Nor is the world badly made because it has much that is hard; it is the best image of the intelligible that there could be.

chapters.title: They rank themselves above the stars
chapters.summary: It is unreasonable for people who have bodies and passions to claim to touch the intelligible, and deny that the sun's soul is better than theirs, or that the heavens share in immortality. Their soul made of the elements cannot live. They hate the world and dream of a "new earth" as its pattern; but where would this pattern come from?

chapters.title: What is new in them is not true
chapters.summary: Their "sojourns", "antitypes" and "repentances" are empty words to found a sect. What is true in them they took from Plato; what is new is false. They misread the Timaeus and multiply intelligible beings. They should take from the ancients what is well said, argue fairly where they differ, and not abuse the Greeks to win a name.

chapters.title: The world-soul is not bound as we are
chapters.summary: The world never began and will not end. Our soul's union with the body is not best for it; but to judge the soul of the universe by ours is like blaming a whole city for its potters. We are bound by the body; the world-soul binds and is not bound, and orders its body without effort. What perishes is like a tortoise caught in a great dance.

chapters.title: The world is a clear image of the intelligible gods
chapters.summary: To ask why soul made the world is to ask why soul exists: it assumes a beginning to what is eternal. The world shows the greatness of the intelligible, a clear and beautiful statue of the intelligible gods; it had to exist, since the intelligible acts both in itself and on another. The stars are gods with virtue; and if souls came here willingly, why blame the place?

chapters.title: Wealth, poverty and wrongdoing; the many gods
chapters.summary: The good man does not seek equality in wealth or power. Wrongdoing comes from souls like children, not from intellect; and there are judgments and punishments here, and gods who watch. We should try to be as good as we can, but not think ourselves the only good ones: there are good daemons and gods, and the world-soul. God's greatness is shown in the many gods he makes. The Gnostics flatter fools: "you are a son of God".

chapters.title: Why Plotinus writes; the fall of Wisdom
chapters.summary: Much more could be examined, but Plotinus writes for his own pupils, out of regard for friends still held by these views, not to persuade the Gnostics. He ends with the most absurd thing: their story that soul and a certain "Wisdom" sank down and lit up the darkness, and that from images of images came the maker of this world.

chapters.title: The image that made the world
chapters.summary: If the soul did not come down but only lit the darkness, how did it sink? Why did it alone shine, and not the higher powers? Why did it wait for images to be born? An image of soul would need no matter. Is the image a substance or a "thought"? Either way, their story of a maker made of images falls apart.

chapters.title: How could an image remember, or plan?
chapters.summary: Their image, just born, could not remember what it never saw; yet they, true souls, scarcely recollect. Nature does not make fire first and then the rest, but outlines the whole animal at once. Foreseeing the heavens and the zodiac is no work of an image. If the lighting of the darkness was natural, it was always; if not, evil was there before the world, and the cause goes back to the first.

chapters.title: Do not fear the spheres
chapters.summary: Whoever blames the world does not know the order of first, second and third. The spheres are not terrors, as the Gnostics' tragedies make them, but bring good things; their bodies are fine and their souls finer. What they do are signs of things to come. Not all can be good; what is less good is not therefore evil, or there would be evil in the intelligible world too.

chapters.title: Magic, and diseases as daemons
chapters.summary: They make the higher beings open to spells, as if words and hissings could charm what is incorporeal. They say diseases are daemons they can drive out; but diseases have bodily causes, and are cured by purging, bleeding and fasting. Our philosophy, by contrast, shows simplicity of character and pure thinking, with dignity, not arrogance.

chapters.title: They teach no virtue
chapters.summary: Of the two schools of the end of life, pleasure and the beautiful, the Gnostics are worse than Epicurus: he removed providence, but they blame its lord, mock the laws and self-control, and leave only pleasure. They say nothing about virtue, what it is or how the soul is purified. "Look to God" helps nothing without being taught how; without true virtue, God is only a name.

chapters.title: To despise the world is not to be good
chapters.summary: Despising the world and its gods does not make anyone good; one who loves the father loves his children too. They say God cares for them alone, but if he is absent from the world he is absent from them. The universe is ordered and wise; no musician or geometer is unmoved by the image of the intelligible he sees here, and whoever is unmoved by the beauty of the stars has not seen the beauty there.

chapters.title: The beauty of the world, inside and out
chapters.summary: If they hate the body because Plato blamed it, they should take the body away in thought and see the intelligible sphere and the souls that give it size. The world-soul gives body all the beauty it can take, without jealousy. Despise the beauty of boys and women if you must, but not the beauty of the whole: the universe was never a child, and nothing bad can be added to it.

chapters.title: Two men in one fine house
chapters.summary: They say their teaching makes people flee the body, and ours keeps the soul in it. It is like two men in a fine house: one finds fault with it and stays; the other praises the builder and waits calmly for the time to leave. We should live in our bodies as the world-soul lives in the whole, untroubled; and not grudge the stars their contemplation, as though they did not see because we do not see their souls.

chapters.title: Can the soul be affected?
chapters.summary: Perceptions are not affections but activities and judgments about them. But how is the soul unchanged, when vice, false opinions, pleasures, pains and desires seem to arise in it? If soul has no size and is to be imperishable, we must not give it such affections; we must think of them as "affections without affection", taken over from bodies by analogy.

chapters.title: Virtue and vice are not alterations
chapters.summary: Virtue is a harmony of the soul's parts, vice a discord; but each part has its own virtue first. Ignorance is an absence; false opinion is like a false sight. Reason "hears" intellect as sight sees: the activity is no alteration. Memory too is a power woken, not a store of imprints. Cowardice, courage and licence are ways each part acts or fails to act, with no change in its substance.

chapters.title: Feelings belong to the body; their source is in soul
chapters.summary: We cannot deny that pleasure, pain, fear and desire are real changes; but we must ask what changes. To say the soul blushes or turns pale would be absurd: the shame or fear begins in soul, the blood changes in the body. Soul's movements come from it, as life does, without alteration; memories and images are not stamped in it like wax.

chapters.title: The affective part is a form, like a harmony
chapters.summary: The affective part is where feelings followed by pleasure and pain arise. Some follow opinion, some come before it. The image in soul starts the trouble, but the trembling and pallor are in the body. The affective part is a form in matter, rooted in the soul of growth; it moves the body as a harmony might move the strings, itself unmoved.

chapters.title: Then why purify the soul?
chapters.summary: If the soul is not affected, why make it free from affection by philosophy? Because the image coming into it is followed by trouble; reason would remove the image, as waking ends a dream. Purification is to leave the soul alone, not looking to other things or holding alien opinions; for the lower part, it is waking from strange images and not leaning down.

chapters.title: Being, and the bodies that seem most real
chapters.summary: Now matter. First, true being is not what most people think: it lacks nothing, is life and intellect, receives nothing, and is all things at once. Bodies and their substrate are not-being. Hard things seem most real because they strike us, but the heavier a thing, the more it falls short; perceiving is the sleep of the soul, and true waking is a rising from bodies.

chapters.title: Matter is a phantom, a mirror of images
chapters.summary: Matter is incorporeal, but not soul, intellect, life, form or power: it is truly not-being, a phantom of bulk, invisible, seen when one does not look. What seems to be in it are images in an image, as in a mirror; they come and go and do nothing to it, as forms might pass through a void. So it stays unaffected.

chapters.title: What is affected must have opposites in it
chapters.summary: What is affected must have qualities opposite to those that come upon it, as heat is altered by cold. When fire perishes, the fire perishes, not the matter; affection is the road to perishing, and matter cannot perish. But how can matter hold so many mingled qualities and not be affected with them?

chapters.title: Things can be present without affecting
chapters.summary: One thing can be present in another in several ways: changing it, improving it without affecting it, or like a shape in wax, or light, which alters nothing. Mirrors are not affected by their images; matter is even less. Only opposites affect opposites; matter has no opposite in it, so it is like a house in which men fight, untouched by the blows.

chapters.title: If matter were altered, it would not stay matter
chapters.summary: If matter were affected, it would keep something of the affection, and become qualified matter, and then many-shaped, no longer able to receive everything, and so perishable. What is altered must remain while it changes; so matter, whose being is to be matter, cannot be altered as matter, any more than a form can be altered in its substance.

chapters.title: How matter shares in form without being changed
chapters.summary: Plato's words, "the things that come in and go out are always imitations of the things that are", point to the puzzle: not how forms come into matter, but how they are in it while it stays unaffected. Matter gains nothing and loses nothing. If it were truly made beautiful it would cease to be matter; it shares only in seeming, and so stays evil, unaffected even by the good.

chapters.title: Plato's figures: matter is not altered by shapes
chapters.summary: Plato makes matter take on figures to show that it stays unaffected: if shapes cause the feelings of living bodies while matter has none, it is not altered by them. His words "burnt" and "made wet" are softened by "receiving the forms of air and water". Fire is not "burnt"; and what has no size cannot be divided.

chapters.title: Receptacle and nurse: matter keeps its nature
chapters.summary: They say matter flees from form; but matter is held in stones and rocks. It "flees" by being always itself, having form as if it never had it. Plato's "receptacle and nurse of all becoming", the "place" and "seat" in which things appear and from which they go, keep it unaffected. What comes into it is an image into what is not true, like a reflection in an invisible mirror.

chapters.title: Poverty, begging at the door
chapters.summary: Without matter, nothing would come to be, as there is no image without a mirror. Matter is the Poverty of Plato's myth: it begs, and takes whatever it is given, and is never filled; it lies with Resource, the wisdom of the image. What it seems to receive slides off it, like an echo, or like light on a burning-glass: it holds nothing and stays itself.

chapters.title: Images that do not mix
chapters.summary: The fire caught in a burning-glass is outside the glass and touches it; the forms are "outside" matter by its otherness alone, not mixing with it, as opinions and images in the soul come and go without mixing. But the soul can push its images away; matter, weaker, has nothing of its own, cannot even say "I am here", and is found only by a deep reasoning.

chapters.title: Size comes and goes, and matter stays
chapters.summary: A rational principle makes matter great by putting greatness round it; take the form away and the substrate is not great. The size of a horse goes with the horse; the size of fire with the fire. If the heaven and all in it ceased, all size would leave matter, which would remain as it was. Matter is all things by sharing, size among them.

chapters.title: The great runs out, and matter runs with it
chapters.summary: Matter is not size itself. The great in intellect and soul wants to be great, and gives its imitators the power to stamp it on another; running out in imaging, it drags matter with it, so that it seems great, stretched but not filled. Each principle images its own size into matter, which stretches to all, lying in the middle between form and nothing.

chapters.title: Like a cloak that can be taken off
chapters.summary: A thought of the great, with power to go outward, would meet a nature with no trace of form, and make it great as an image. Matter keeps its nature, wearing this greatness like a cloak it put on while running; take it off and it is as it was. Soul receives forms without bulk; matter, a shadow with no activity of its own, waits to suffer what the maker wills, and receives all things, but in parts.

chapters.title: The mother that does not beget
chapters.summary: What comes into matter, its "mother", neither harms nor helps it; qualities affect one another, and living bodies are affected, but matter stays. "Receptacle and nurse" suit it better than "mother", for it begets nothing. So the ancient wise men, in their rites, showed Hermes with the organ of generation, and the Mother of all with sterile attendants: matter receives, but does not beget.

chapters.title: Where to begin
chapters.summary: We think we understand eternity and time until we look closely; then we fall back on the ancients' opinions. Some of the ancients found the truth; we must ask who, and how we may understand. We begin with eternity, the pattern, for then its image, time, may be clear; or one may start from time and climb by recollection to what it is like.

chapters.title: Eternity is not intelligible being, nor rest
chapters.summary: Is eternity the intelligible substance itself, as some say time is the heaven? Both are most venerable, both contain all; but we say the pattern is "eternal", so eternity is something about it. Nor is it rest: rest is not eternal of itself, motion there is eternal too, and eternity must be one and without extension, which rest is not.

chapters.title: Eternity is life all at once
chapters.summary: What makes the intelligible world eternal is something gathered from many, and yet one: substance, motion, rest, otherness and sameness, brought together into one life. Eternity is that life, unceasing and the same, holding all things present at once, with nothing past and nothing to come: what neither was nor will be, but only is.

chapters.title: Eternity is from being, and with it
chapters.summary: Eternity is not an accident of being, but from it and with it, as truth and beauty are. The true whole lacks nothing, so nothing can come to it: no "will be". Things that come to be need their future to be what they are, and hasten towards it; the universe moves in a circle out of longing for being. The first beings long for nothing. Eternity is named from "always being".

chapters.title: Contemplating eternity, one becomes eternal
chapters.summary: To see eternity is to see what has never had anything happen to it, always the same, so that whenever you look you find it so. One who never stopped looking, with a tireless nature, would himself stand in eternity. Eternity is the being with this condition showing in it: venerable, the same as God, a god showing himself as he is; an infinite life that loses nothing.

chapters.title: "Eternity remaining in one"
chapters.summary: Plato rightly said eternity "remains in one": the life of being around the One, true being that never is not and never is otherwise, with no before or after. "Always" is said only for clearness, as "true" is added to "philosopher". What is in time, however complete, still needs what comes next; eternity needs nothing. Plato's "he was good" refers to the whole, not to a beginning in time.

chapters.title: From eternity down to time
chapters.summary: We could not speak of eternity unless we had a share in it. To see how we are in time and in eternity, we must go down to time, as time itself came down. The ancients' views of time fall into three: it is motion, or what is moved, or something of motion: its interval, its number or measure, or what follows it.

chapters.title: Time is not motion, nor the interval of motion
chapters.summary: Time is not motion: motions are in time, and can stop, while time cannot; the heaven's circuit takes time, half a circuit half the time. Nor is it the sphere. Nor the interval of motion: motions of the same kind differ in speed, and are measured by something else; the interval in a motion is only its quantity, and that is in time; and rest has a duration too.

chapters.title: Time is not the number or measure of motion
chapters.summary: If time is the number or measure of motion, of which motion? The same number for orderly and disorderly, fast and slow, would be like ten measuring horses and oxen: it says what time measures, not what it is. A measure running along with motion, or a number "according to before and after", already presupposes time; and time, being without limit, would exist before it was measured, even before a soul measured it.

chapters.title: What follows motion
chapters.summary: To call time something that follows motion does not say what it is before saying what follows; and whatever this is, it is said to be in time. Enough of reviewing others; the views already answered serve against the rest. We must now say what time is.

chapters.title: Time born when soul set out from eternity
chapters.summary: Go back to eternity, the still, whole, unlimited life. Time was not yet. A restless power of soul, wanting to rule itself and seek more than the present, moved, and time moved with it. As a seed unfolds into a weaker length, soul, making the world in imitation, made itself temporal in place of eternity and put the world under time. Time is the life of soul in a motion passing from one way of life to another: the image of eternity, one by continuity, unlimited by always going on, a whole by parts, in soul as eternity is in being.

chapters.title: The heavens show time; they do not make it
chapters.summary: Time is the length of soul's life going on in smooth, silent changes. If soul turned back to eternity and was still, time would be gone, and the sphere with it: so soul's motion and life produce time, which is why Plato says time came to be with the universe. The motions of the stars were made to show and mark off time, the day and night giving the idea of number; time is not itself a measure, and is measured by the circuit only incidentally, as a magnitude is "what a cubit measures".

chapters.title: Time is in soul, as eternity is in being
chapters.summary: The circuit shows the time it is in; time itself is first, the "in which" of all else. The philosophers called it the measure of motion, putting the incidental for the essential; Plato says only that it came to be with the heaven as a moving image of eternity. Soul's own motion is first in time and produces it, and is everywhere in the world. Bodily motion leads back to soul's motion, and that to the unextended. Time is in every soul of this kind alike, and all are one, so time is not torn apart.

chapters.title: Divided and undivided being
chapters.summary: There is being wholly divided, as bodies are, and being wholly undivided, needing no place, like the centre from which the lines of a circle go out. Next to bodies are forms and qualities, divided in them but whole in each piece. Next to the undivided is soul: a being that gives itself to bodies and is divided about them, yet remains one, whole in all their parts and whole in any part. The division belongs to the bodies, not to the soul.

chapters.title: Why the soul must be both
chapters.summary: If the soul were divided like a body, the soul in the finger would feel its own pain and no other part would; there would be many souls in each of us. The Stoic account of sensations passed on to a ruling part fails: which part feels, and how could one know a thing from eyes and ears together? If soul were wholly one, it would animate nothing. So soul is one and many, as Plato's "third kind of being" says: soul one and many, forms in bodies many and one, bodies many only, the highest one only.

chapters.title: Are our souls parts of the world's soul?
chapters.summary: Nothing is more worth inquiring into than the soul, for it gives knowledge of what comes from it and what it comes from, and the god bids us know ourselves. Some say our souls come from the soul of the universe, as parts: they are like in kind, Plato said our body is part of the world's body and so our soul part of its soul, we follow its circuit and take our characters from it, and "all soul cares for all that is without soul".

chapters.title: In what sense a part?
chapters.summary: Not a part as of a body, nor as two is part of ten, nor as an arc of a circle: soul is not a quantity, and all souls are said to be alike and whole. Perhaps as a theorem is part of a science, which stays whole while each theorem has it all potentially. But then the whole soul belongs to nothing, not even to the world; the world's soul too is one of the parts. Why, then, is one the world's?

chapters.title: Not as the soul in a finger
chapters.summary: Is it a part as the soul in a finger is part of the whole animal's soul? That would leave no soul outside body, or the world's soul outside the world's body. If the world's soul gives itself to each living thing, it is undivided, the same in many, and there is no whole and part; as in us the same soul is in eye and ear, with different powers acting because the organs differ, and one judge of all.

chapters.title: One soul in all, some in bodies, some not
chapters.summary: If all souls are one, how is one in body and another not? With intellect there is no difficulty, but with soul there is, unless one soul stays above and the world's soul and ours come from it, joined at their upper edge and reaching down here and there, like light divided among houses. The world's soul never comes down; ours have a part marked off here and turn to what needs care: the world's lowest soul is like the soul in a great plant, ours like worms in a rotten part of it, or like a gardener caring for them.

chapters.title: Socrates will not perish above
chapters.summary: How will this soul be yours and that one his? Socrates is Socrates while his soul is in body; will he perish when he comes to the best? No: nothing that is perishes. Up there the minds do not perish, since they are not divided like bodies into one, but each remains what it is in otherness. So too souls, hanging from each intellect, are rational forms of minds, unfolded further, and stay each one and all one.

chapters.title: Why the world's soul made the world
chapters.summary: Why did the world's soul make the world and ours did not, though it is of the same form? Those with the same science may rule more or fewer. The world's soul did not leave the whole and had the body about it while there; ours took their lots when their sister had already prepared their dwellings. It looks to the whole intellect, they to their particular ones. Power is greater the more it stays above; ours were drawn down. Plato's "second and third" mean nearer and further.

chapters.title: What Plato meant
chapters.summary: The Philebus says only that the heaven has a soul, since we, parts of its body, have souls. The Timaeus makes our souls later, from the same bowl, second and third; the Phaedrus distinguishes the perfect soul that rides above from the one that sheds its wings. Following the circuit and taking our characters from it no more makes us parts than taking them from places, waters, air and cities; and we set another soul against these influences, as a child in the womb has a soul other than its mother's.

chapters.title: How souls differ, and the number of them
chapters.summary: Souls are in sympathy, since all come from the one the world's comes from. They differ by bodies, by characters and by earlier lives; and by nature, as each is active with one power or another. They are an ordered whole of fixed number, since true beings stand fast and are each one in number; their unlimitedness is in power. Soul reaches through the whole body without being torn apart, and when an animal rots and many come from it, the one soul is not multiplied.

chapters.title: How soul comes into body
chapters.summary: Soul enters body in two ways: from one body into another, or from being without body into body. Begin with the world's soul, though there was never a time when the world had no soul: the separation is for teaching. Soul, shining out like a great light, made darkness at its edge, saw it, and gave it form. The world is like a fine house that its maker never leaves; it lies in soul like a net in the sea, which spreads as far as it can, while soul is as great as it is because it has no size.

chapters.title: Soul orders the world by nature, not by art
chapters.summary: Think of it all at once: air and light, sun and moon, in order first, second and third, with soul standing always, and its light reaching to the dim edge. Soul orders body by its rational forms, as forms in seeds shape animals like little worlds, not by deliberation, which belongs to art, the weak late imitator. Soul is master of bodies; whatever it makes it makes from what it has, and as fire warms, soul gives life, a living rational form, an image of its own life, and the forms of all things, gods too.

chapters.title: Statues of the gods
chapters.summary: The ancient sages, who made temples and statues wanting the gods to be present, saw that soul is easy to draw anywhere, and easiest to receive in something made to be in sympathy, like a mirror catching a form. Nature made everything in imitation of the forms, linking each to the god after whom it came to be. That god is intellect, the sun there; soul hangs from it and links the sun here to the sun there, as an interpreter between them. The heavenly gods are gods because they never stand apart from that one.

chapters.title: Souls of men come down, heads above heaven
chapters.summary: Seeing their images as Dionysus saw his in the mirror, men's souls rushed down, still not cut off from intellect: they reach the earth, but their head is set above heaven. Their middle part had to care for what they came to. Zeus, pitying their labours, made their bonds mortal and gave them rests free of bodies. The order of the whole joins descents and ascents in one harmony, signified by the stars; souls come down more or less, each into what is ready for it, by likeness.

chapters.title: The descent as a law of nature
chapters.summary: What is inescapable, and justice, lie in a ruling nature: each goes in order to what it has become an image of. No one sends a soul down; at its time it goes as of itself, as if called by a herald, as if drawn by magic, as in an animal beard and horns come at their times, and trees bloom. It is neither willing nor sent: willing as a leap by nature, not by choice. The law is not outside; those who carry it fulfil it when the time comes, weighed down by it and longing to go where it calls.

chapters.title: Pandora and Prometheus
chapters.summary: With souls coming down, the world has many lights and is adorned with gifts from the gods and the other minds. The myth riddles this: when Prometheus had shaped the woman, the other gods adorned her, each giving a gift, and she was named for all the gifts. Prometheus refusing the gift means that the choice of the intelligible is better; the maker is bound because he touches what he made, and Heracles frees him because he has the power.

chapters.title: Down through the heavens
chapters.summary: Souls peep out of the intelligible first into heaven, take a body there, and go on into earthier ones, as far as they stretch. Some go from body to body, too weighed with forgetfulness to rise. They differ by bodies, fortunes, upbringing, or of themselves. Some are wholly under the fate here, some at times, and some bear what must be borne but keep their own works their own, living by the other law that governs all beings.

chapters.title: Undeserved sufferings
chapters.summary: Punishments of the wicked are justly put down to the order. What of evils that befall the good, without justice? Perhaps they come from past wrongs; or they are not from the leading rational forms but follow on them, like a man killed by a falling house; or the wrong is no evil to the sufferer and useful to the whole. Nothing is left loose: what is unjust for the doer is not unjust in the whole, and if the sufferer is good, it ends in good. The causes are hidden, and give the ignorant cause to blame.

chapters.title: Light from light, and the pilots
chapters.summary: Souls go first into heaven because it is the best of the perceptible and borders on the intelligible; earth is last. All souls shine on heaven and give it most; those that go further down light up lower things, not to their own good. A centre, a circle of light round it, another light from light, then a sphere with no light of its own. Souls tending what they light up are like pilots in a storm who forget themselves and go down with the ship, held at last by the spell of caring for nature.

chapters.title: Do souls reason there, or speak?
chapters.summary: Reasoning comes in here, where soul is in difficulty and full of care: needing it is a lessening of intellect, as craftsmen reason only when stuck. Souls there are rational because they could reason if needed, or if reasoning means the settled activity from intellect. Nor do they use voices in the intelligible, or even with bodies in heaven; they know each other's minds, as we know much from the eyes of the silent, for there every body is pure and each is like an eye. Daemons and souls in the air may well use voice.

chapters.title: Undivided and divided in one soul?
chapters.summary: Are the undivided and the divided in soul mixed in the same thing, or is the divided a second part? Plato calls one simply undivided, the other "becoming divided about bodies". The perceiving, growing and desiring powers are divided as the body is; reasoning and intellect do not give themselves to body, which only hinders their work. So they are two, a whole of pure parts; yet the divided may get its undividedness from the power above, and so be both.

chapters.title: Soul is not in body as in a place
chapters.summary: Is soul, or any part of it, in a place? If no part is, the body is soulless; if some are, not all our soul is in us. Soul is not in body as in a place, which holds a body part by part; nor as in a vessel or an empty extension; nor as an attribute in a subject; nor as part in whole or whole in parts; nor as form in matter. We say it is in body because body is seen and soul not; if soul were seen, we would say the body is in it.

chapters.title: Not like a pilot in a ship
chapters.summary: How, then, is soul present? The pilot in a ship is well said for its separability, but the pilot is not in the whole ship. Perhaps as the steering skill would be in the rudder, if the rudder had a soul: a pilot gone into the rudder, as soul is in body as in a natural instrument. That is another way, but still we must go nearer.

chapters.title: As light is present to air
chapters.summary: Perhaps soul is present to body as fire, or light, is present to air: present without being mixed, staying while the air flows past. So it is more right to say the air is in the light than the light in the air, as Plato set the body of the world in its soul. Only the powers the body needs are present to it, and not settled in its parts: the perceiving power to all that perceives, and different powers for different works.

chapters.title: Where the powers are said to be
chapters.summary: The ensouled body is lit by soul, and each part takes the power fitting its organ: sight in the eyes, hearing in the ears, touch everywhere. The nerves start from the brain, so the ancients put the source of perception and impulse there: not the power, which is everywhere, but the start of its activity. Reason sits above the perceiving and imagining soul, which borders on it, so they set it in the head. Desire is at the liver, where blood and growth begin; spirit at the heart, the spring of the fine, hot blood.

chapters.title: Where the soul goes after death
chapters.summary: Out of the body, soul goes where there is something to receive it, or to a body drawn by something unreasoning in it. Its disposition and the justice in things send it to its place; no one escapes, for the divine law carries out its own judgment, and the wrongdoer, carried unknowing, falls at last where he must, by a willing motion into unwilling suffering. Pure souls, having no body, are where being and the divine are, in God. Ask where those are, and not with the eyes.

chapters.title: What in us remembers?
chapters.summary: Do souls that leave remember, and what, and for how long? First ask what remembers. Memory is of something acquired, so not of God, being or intellect, which are in eternity, with no before and after; intellect knows the changes of the world without remembering, and does not remember its own thoughts, which never came or go. When the ancients spoke of soul's remembering and recollection, they meant its acting on what it has, a memory without time. Is memory the higher soul's, a lower one's, or the compound's?

chapters.title: Memory belongs to soul, not body
chapters.summary: Perceiving is shared, as boring or weaving is, soul the craftsman and body the tool; but memory need not be, since soul keeps or lets go of the impression. Body only helps or hinders. The living being is not a third thing in which soul is potential; if it were, memory would still be soul's, as sweetness in mead is from the honey. Impressions are not like seals in wax, and soul remembers its own desires and thoughts, which never reached the body. Body, flowing, causes forgetting: that is the river of Lethe.

chapters.title: Which soul? The shade of Heracles
chapters.summary: Each soul, the more divine one that we are and the other from the whole, has its memories, some its own, some shared. Apart, each keeps its own longer and the other's briefly. Heracles' shade in Hades remembers all the deeds of his life, since the life was chiefly its; Heracles himself, what he said is not told. The soul freed from body remembers this life, and with time earlier lives too, letting some go; in another body it forgets much. But first: which power remembers?

chapters.title: Not the desiring or spirited part
chapters.summary: Is it the power by which we perceive and learn, or the desiring and spirited parts, since what enjoys should remember? The desiring part is stirred again by what it enjoyed, but that is not memory: sight sees and desire is moved by passing on, without knowing what moved it, as a dog stirs at the scent of a wolf the shepherd has seen. The desiring part keeps a trace as a disposition; something else saw the enjoyment and remembers it, since memory often does not know what desire shared in.

chapters.title: Memory belongs to imagination
chapters.summary: Is memory the perceiving power's? But then, if the shade remembers, there would be two perceiving powers; and the same people are not best at perceiving and at remembering. Rather, what is perceived becomes an image for the imagining power, where perception ends; it keeps the sight when the thing is gone, and that is remembering. A strong imagination remembers long. People differ in memory by their powers, by practice, and by bodily blends.

chapters.title: Memory of thoughts
chapters.summary: What of the memory of thoughts? If an image goes with every thought, memory would be of that. Or rather the thought, partless and within, is unnoticed until a verbal expression unfolds it into the imagining power, which shows it as in a mirror; then we grasp it, keep it and remember it. So we are always thinking, but do not always grasp that we are, because what receives receives perceptions as well, from the other side.

chapters.title: Two imaginations
chapters.summary: If memory is imagination's and both souls remember, there are two imaginations. In us, when they agree, the better rules and one image comes about, the other following like a shadow, a small light under a greater; when they conflict, the lower shows itself, and we notice the doubleness of soul. Going out, the higher keeps some memories and lets go of the other's, as we remember little of poor company once we have found better.

chapters.title: The good soul forgets
chapters.summary: What of friends, children, wife and country? The lower soul remembers them with feeling, the good soul without. The lower longs to remember the higher's doings; the higher gladly forgets the lower's. The more it hastens upward, the more it forgets, unless its whole life here was such as to remember only the better. So the good soul is rightly called forgetful: it flees the many and gathers them into one. Heracles' shade may tell his brave deeds; the one who has gone to the intelligible, stronger than Heracles in the contests of the wise, what will he remember?

chapters.title: Man is soul and body; the soul is the man
chapters.summary: Are we immortal, or do we perish whole, or does part of us go and part stay? Man is not simple: he has a soul and a body. The body is composite, and both reason and perception show it coming apart; even simple bodies have form and matter and can be cut. So if the body is a part of us we are not wholly immortal; if it is a tool, it was given for a time. What is most sovereign, the man himself, is the soul, whether as form to matter or as user to tool.

chapters.title: No body has life of itself
chapters.summary: If the soul is a body, it can be broken up. Into what? If into bodies, either one has life of itself, and that is soul, or none does. Fire, air, water and earth have no life of their own, nor do the elements before them. A coming together of lifeless bodies cannot make life, nor mindless things mind; and a mixture needs something to order it, which has the rank of soul. Even a simple body needs a rational form coming to matter, and that can come only from soul.

chapters.title: Not atoms, not form as an affection of matter
chapters.summary: Atoms put side by side make no unity and no sympathy, and partless things make no body. If life comes from the form in a body, either the form is a being, and that is soul and no body, or it is an affection of matter, and then something gave it. So the giver of life is outside all bodily nature. Without soul's power, body would flow away; even the world would come apart if left to a body, such as their scattered breath, called soul in name only.

chapters.title: The Stoics' breath "in a certain state"
chapters.summary: Even the Stoics, led by truth, admit something before bodies, an intelligent breath and an intellectual fire, but then look for a place for the better, when bodies should be set in soul. If soul is breath "in a certain state", that state is either nothing, and only matter is real, soul and God mere names; or a being, a rational form, not a body. Besides, a body has one quality and does one thing, as fire heats; soul does contrary things in the same animal.

chapters.title: Growth, memory, and parts of soul
chapters.summary: A body has one motion, but soul moves in many, by choice and by rational forms, which are not bodily. A body cannot make itself grow; and if soul were a growing body, what is added would be a new, ignorant soul, and we would keep no memories, since nothing in it would stay the same. Cut a quantity and it is no longer what it was; but each part of soul is a whole soul, and from one seed come twins. So soul and the rational forms are without quantity.

chapters.title: Perception needs something undivided
chapters.summary: If the soul were a body, there would be no perceiving, thinking, knowing, virtue or anything fine. What perceives must be one, taking in a face whole, and sight and hearing together, like a centre where the lines from a circle meet. If it had size, it would be divided with its object, and no one would perceive the whole; or each piece would perceive the whole, making images without limit. And impressions in a body would either run together, as in water, so that there is no memory, or block new ones.

chapters.title: Pain in the finger
chapters.summary: When a man has a pain in his finger, the pain is in the finger but the perceiving is in the ruling part. If the Stoic breath passes the affection along, each stage would feel its own pain, and the ruling part would feel only the pain next to it, not the finger's. Since one piece of a mass cannot know what another undergoes, what perceives must be the same with itself everywhere: something other than body.

chapters.title: Thinking, virtue; not a harmony, not an entelechy
chapters.summary: Thinking grasps without body what has no size, and abstracts circle and line from matter, so what thinks is no body; the beautiful, the just and the virtues are without size and everlasting, and need something lasting to be in. Bodies act by bodiless powers; qualities are not bodies; a body cannot pass whole through a body, but soul does. The Stoics put nature before soul and intellect last, the worse before the better. Nor is soul a harmony, which comes after and cannot rule; nor an inseparable entelechy, for soul withdraws in sleep, opposes desire, thinks, and moves from body to body. It is a true being.

chapters.title: Being from itself, life from itself
chapters.summary: The other nature has being from itself: all that really is, which neither comes to be nor perishes, and which keeps all else safe. Soul is a principle of motion, moving itself and giving life to the ensouled body, having its life from itself, so it never loses it. Not all life can be borrowed; there must be something living first, imperishable. What is from itself is always, as whiteness is never not white; and it is not dead like a stone, but lives a pure life, hindered when mixed with the worse, but never losing its nature.

chapters.title: The soul is akin to the divine
chapters.summary: Soul is akin to the divine and everlasting: it has no body, shape or colour. Take soul not with the desires and passions of the body, but purified: then wisdom and the other virtue are seen to be its own, and evils added from outside. If all souls were like this, no one would doubt immortality. Look at yourself, with the additions taken away: you will see intellect seeing the everlasting, lit by truth from the Good, and say "Farewell: I am an immortal god to you." Like living gold cleaned of earth, it wonders at itself.

chapters.title: Life that cannot be lost
chapters.summary: Who with sense would doubt that such a thing is immortal? Its life is not acquired, nor present as heat to fire, which belongs to the fire's matter, so that fire can be put out. Either life is the soul's being, a being that lives of itself, which they will grant is immortal; or, if they break it up, they must come at last to something immortal, moved of itself; or, if life is an affection brought into matter, what brought it must be immortal, unable to take the opposite of what it brings.

chapters.title: All souls are immortal
chapters.summary: If every soul perished, all would long since have perished. If the world's soul is immortal and ours not, why? Each is a principle of motion, lives of itself, and thinks the same things, in heaven and beyond, up to the first principle. Its knowledge, by recollection, gives it being before the body, and its everlasting knowledge shows it everlasting. It is simple, so it is not dissolved; it has no mass, so it is not cut up; and alteration takes away form and leaves matter, which belongs to composites.

chapters.title: Why soul comes into body
chapters.summary: If the intelligible is separate, why does soul come into body? Intellect alone stays above, without impulse or desire. What has desire, next to intellect, goes out further: longing to order things by what it saw in intellect, as if pregnant, it hastens to make. With the soul of the whole it presides from outside; wanting to govern a part, it comes into it, yet not wholly, keeping something outside body. It is now in body, now out, set in motion from the first, going to the third, by the act of intellect, which stays and fills all with beauty through soul.

chapters.title: Souls of animals and plants
chapters.summary: Souls that went astray as far as beasts' bodies are immortal too; and if there is another kind of soul, in animals and plants, it comes from the living nature, the same principle, and is bodiless, partless and a being. If the human soul, being in three parts, is broken up with the compound, the pure souls leave behind what was moulded on in birth, and the others keep it long; and even the worse part is not destroyed while its source is. Nothing that is perishes.

chapters.title: Evidence from oracles and the dead
chapters.summary: That is the proof for those who need proof. For those who want belief mixed with perception, there is much in history: the gods' oracles bidding men appease the wrath of wronged souls and honour the dead as still perceiving, as all men do; and many souls that were once in men have not stopped doing good to men out of the body, giving oracles and showing by themselves that other souls have not perished either.

chapters.title: Why souls forget their father
chapters.summary: Souls forget God their father, and themselves, because of daring, birth, the first otherness, and the wish to be their own. Delighting in moving by themselves, they ran the other way, like children taken from their parents, and, admiring what is here, they despised themselves. Two lessons are needed: one showing how worthless what they now honour is, the other reminding the soul of its race and worth, which comes first.

chapters.title: The soul that animates the heaven
chapters.summary: Let every soul remember that it made all living things, the sun and this great heaven, and orders and moves them, being other than they and more honourable, since they perish when soul leaves them and it does not leave itself. Let a quiet soul, with body, earth, sea and sky at rest, think of soul flowing into the heaven from outside like sunlight into a dark cloud, giving it life and immortality. It is whole everywhere, and makes the world a god, and the sun and stars. Ours is of the same form: admire yourself.

chapters.title: Soul is an image of intellect
chapters.summary: Soul, honourable and divine as it is, is an image of intellect, as spoken words are of the thought in the soul: it is the rational expression and activity of intellect, as fire has heat in itself and heat it gives. So it is intellectual, its intellect working in reasonings, and perfected by intellect as by a father. Its own activities are the intellectual ones; the worse come from elsewhere. Nothing comes between them but otherness: soul receives, intellect is form.

chapters.title: Intellect, the true world
chapters.summary: Admire this world, its size and order, its gods, daemons, animals and plants, then go up to its archetype: all things there are intelligible and everlasting, with pure intellect over them, a life truly under Cronos. It has all things at rest, needs no change, thinks by having, not seeking; it is eternity, which time imitates. Each thing there is intellect and being: intellect makes being exist by thinking it, being gives intellect its thinking. Their cause is another. The first kinds are intellect, being, otherness, sameness, motion and rest; from them number and quality.

chapters.title: Number and the indefinite two
chapters.summary: This god, intellect, is many, and the soul, joined to it, asks: who begot it, the simple one before it, the cause of its being many, maker of number? Number is not first: before the two is the One, and the two, indefinite of itself, is defined by the One and becomes number, number as being. Soul too is number. In the intelligible the two and number are rational forms and intellect: the indefinite two is like the substrate, and the number from it and the One are the forms. Intellect is shaped both by the One and by itself, like sight in act.

chapters.title: How intellect comes from the One
chapters.summary: How did the many come from the One, and why did it not stay by itself? Let us call on God, not with words but stretching the soul in prayer, alone to the alone. Set aside coming to be in time. What comes from the One comes without its moving, consenting or willing: a radiance around it, like the sun's light, while it stays. Everything that is complete produces an image of itself, as fire gives heat and perfumes their scent; the always complete produces the everlasting, and less than itself. After the One comes intellect, which sees it and needs it alone; then soul, the expression of intellect.

chapters.title: Intellect, the image of the One
chapters.summary: Intellect is the One's image, keeping much of it, as light keeps the sun. How does the One produce intellect, not being intellect? Turning to it, intellect saw, and the seeing is intellect. The One is the power of all things; intellect, thinking, splits that power into the things, and defines its own being by it. Because the One is none of all things, all come from it. Intellect produces the beings with itself, the beauty of the forms and the intelligible gods, and keeps them, as Cronos swallowed his children; then, complete, it produces soul, as Cronos fathered Zeus.

chapters.title: Plato and Parmenides had the three
chapters.summary: So Plato has his triads: "all things about the king of all, the second about the second, the third about the third". The cause is intellect, his maker, who makes the soul in the bowl, and its father is the Good, beyond intellect and being. These doctrines are not new: they were said of old, not spelled out, and ours interpret them. Parmenides joined being and thinking, and called it one, unmoved, like a sphere; Plato's Parmenides, more exactly, distinguishes the first One, the one-many, and the one and many.

chapters.title: The other ancients
chapters.summary: Anaxagoras' pure, unmixed intellect makes the first simple and the One separate, but he was too early to be exact. Heraclitus knew the One everlasting and intelligible; with Empedocles, love is the One. Aristotle makes the first separate and intelligible, but by making it think itself he makes it not first; and his many movers of the spheres are either from one, and so an intelligible world, or many principles by chance. The Pythagoreans and Pherecydes had this nature in view, some in writing, some in unwritten teaching.

chapters.title: The three are in us too
chapters.summary: Beyond being is the One; next, being and intellect; third, soul. As they are in nature, so they are in us, not in the perceptible part but outside it, in what Plato calls the inner man. Our soul is divine, perfect when it has intellect; its reasoning part needs no bodily organ and should be placed among the first intelligibles, outside place. So Plato set soul around the world from outside, and our head above the heaven; and the separation he urges is not in place but in not inclining to body.

chapters.title: The just itself, and God, in us
chapters.summary: The soul reasons whether this is just or that beautiful, so there must be something just that stands still, from which reasoning comes. Since the soul does not always reason, there must be in us an intellect that always has the just, and also the principle and cause of intellect, God: not divided, staying, seen in each thing able to receive it, as the centre is in itself while each radius has a point in it. By this in us we touch it and hang from it, and settle there when we incline to it.

chapters.title: Why we do not notice them
chapters.summary: If we have such great things, why do we not notice them? They are always active, intellect and what is before intellect, and soul's ever-moving part; but what is in the soul reaches us only when it comes to perception, and we are with the perceiving part, not the whole soul. To grasp them we must turn our attention inward, as one who waits for a voice he wants to hear sets the others aside and listens: we must keep the soul's power of grasping pure and ready to hear the sounds from above.

chapters.title: The One overflows
chapters.summary: The One is all things and not one of them: their principle, not they. How does the varied come from what is simple? Because nothing is in it, all comes from it; to produce being it is not being. Perfect, needing nothing, it overflowed; what came to be turned to it, was filled, and looking at it became intellect: its standing towards the One made being, its looking made intellect. Intellect poured out power in turn, and soul came to be while intellect stayed; soul, moving, produced its image, perception and the nature in plants, nothing cut off from what is before it.

chapters.title: A long life stretched out
chapters.summary: Each thing stays in its seat while what it produces takes a lower rank, and each becomes the same as what it follows, while it follows. In a plant the boldest, least sensible part of soul has come this far; in a beast perception rules; in man reason or intellect. Cut a branch or burn a root, and the soul there goes back to its source, not to another place, since none of these are in place. All of this is that one and not that one. It is like one long life stretched out, each part other, all continuous.

chapters.title: Can the simple think itself?
chapters.summary: Must what thinks itself be varied, seeing the rest of itself by one part, as if the wholly simple could not turn to itself? If it thinks itself because it is composite, seeing the rest by one part, it does not really think itself: one thing sees another. We cannot give up the view that something truly thinks itself: intellect would be absurd if it knew all else and not itself. Perception knows the outside; intellect knows the intelligibles. Does it know itself as well, and how?

chapters.title: Does the soul know itself?
chapters.summary: First the soul. Its perceiving part knows only what is outside, even when it perceives the body's affections. Its reasoning part judges the images from perception, joins and divides them, and looks at the imprints coming from intellect, fitting new ones to old: these are the soul's recollections. Does this part turn to itself and know itself? If so, it is intellect, and we must ask how it differs from intellect above; if not, we must go up to that.

chapters.title: We are the reasoning part
chapters.summary: Perception sees a man and gives the imprint to thought, which knows him and, with memory, says "Socrates"; asked whether he is good, it judges by a rule of the good it has from intellect shining on it. It is still soul, for soul is in reasonings. Pure intellect is ours and not ours: above the reasoning part, used and not used. We are the reasoning part, the middle between perception below and intellect above; perception is always ours, intellect is disputed, because it does not lean towards us, but we look up to it. Perception is our messenger, intellect our king.

chapters.title: Two ways of knowing ourselves
chapters.summary: We are kings too when we are in accordance with intellect, by its laws written in us, or filled with it, or seeing it present.
